I once worked on a C compiler for the IBM 1401 for an academic project. Now, C is a wonderful language, and the compiler was written in Java, which is not too terrible, but, when it came to code generation, we had to work with the 1401's Autocoder assembly, which is an utter nightmare of a language. The syntax of the language is not too terrible as far as assembly languages go, except that each line had to be formatted to fit on a punchcard. However, as the code would ultimately run on an IBM 1401, a machine designed before the integrated circuit and well before any of our modern notions on how computers ought to work, some of the design decisions were rather interesting:

  • Addressable "bytes" were eight bits each. However, these eight bits included a word marker (more on that later) and a parity bit (for error detection), leaving six usable bits and 64 possible values. This is weird.

  • Numeric values were encoded in binary coded decimal. This means that, of the 64 possible values of a "byte", ten of them represented the digits 0-9. If I wanted to encode the number 16, for example, one byte would represent the digit "1", and the next would represent the digit "6".

  • All data were variable sized. A pointer to a datum would be the address of the last digit/"byte" of that datum. The datum would consist of all digits between that last one and the first preceding digit which had its word marker set.

  • Memory addresses were encoded differently than numbers. Like I said before, numbers were encoded in binary coded decimal. Memory addresses below 1000 were encoded in the same manner. However, memory addresses were universally 3 digits long, so different conventions were followed for addresses over 999. Since only 4 out of 6 bits are needed to code for the numbers 0 - 9, the other two bits of the first and third digits of an address were modulated in order to account for the other 15000 possible addresses.

  • There were no registers. Since the 1401 was developed before integrated circuits, let alone CPUs, all memory was universally slow. While a modern CPU contains a bunch of lightning fast registers for storing values that are being looked up and changing a lot, the 1401 had no such notion. All instructions worked directly on values in memory. This was actually pretty cool to be honest.
